html:
The Wari Empire was an Andean state centred on the Ayacucho basin of the Peruvian highlands, which grew from about 600 CE to control much of highland and coastal Peru before fading around 1000 to 1100. It is often called the first Andean empire.

Its capital, also called Wari, was a large walled city near modern Ayacucho. From there the Wari built provincial centres across Peru, such as Pikillacta near Cusco, laid out as rigid grids of identical rooms and courtyards. They seem to have been places to store food, house workers and hold feasts that bound local people to the state. Roads linked them, and some of these routes were later reused by the Inca road system.

Wari spread farming on terraces and kept records on knotted strings, forerunners of the Inca quipu. Its art shared a staff god with Tiwanaku, its neighbour to the south near Lake Titicaca, though the two were separate powers. Wari took over the south coast after the decline of the Nazca, and its reach on the north coast came after the Moche.

Wari broke up around 1000, perhaps in part through drought, leaving regional kingdoms. Later the Inca used many of the same methods of rule: provincial centres, roads, storehouses and labour service.
